fact_en: Different reflecting surfaces produce different image characteristics, such as being upright or inverted, larger or smaller, and real or virtual.
fact_bis: Ang lain-laing reflecting surface naghimo og lain-laing kinaiya sa imahe, sama sa pagtindog o bali, mas dako o mas gamay, ug real o virtual.

findings.note: Image Characteristics. EN pairs are "upright or inverted", "larger or smaller", "real or virtual"; the Cebuano gives "pagtindog o bali". Cebuano bali = broken/fractured, so the contrast reads "standing up or broken" — a false property of mirror images, and the inverted concept is lost and never restored in the card. Inverted is baliskad / balit-ad. Lower confidence than dcard-00614: some speakers use bali-bali loosely for reversed, but bare bali in a science list reads as broken.

fact_en: The skeletal system supports the body, protects internal organs like the heart and lungs, enables movement, stores minerals like calcium, and supplies red and white blood cells.
fact_bis: Ang skeletal system mosuporta sa lawas, moprotektar sa mga internal organs sama sa kasingkasing ug baga, magpaliwat, magtipig ug minerals sama sa calcium, ug maghimo ug red ug white blood cells.

findings.note: Skeletal System Functions. EN lists five functions including "enables movement"; the Cebuano renders that item as "magpaliwat" — Cebuano paliwat = to breed/propagate offspring, not to move. The card therefore tells a child the skeleton "reproduces/breeds", and the movement function is dropped entirely with nothing elsewhere in the card restoring it. Correct word is motabang sa paglihok — which the corpus's own parallel card dcard-00603 (same function list) uses: "motabang sa paglihok".

fact_en: Optical fibers are thin strands that carry visible light, and one medical use is the endoscope, a flexible tube with a tiny camera used to observe the internal parts of the body.
fact_bis: Ang optical fibers mga nipis nga mga hilo nga nagdala sa visible light, ug usa ka gamit sa medisina mao ang endoscope, usa ka flexible tube nga adunay gagmay nga camera aron makita ang mga sulod nga parte sa lawas.

findings.note: bis renders "Optical fibers are thin strands" as "Ang optical fibers mga nipis nga mga hilo". In Cebuano hilo = POISON/VENOM (correct Cebuano for thread/fibre is tanod or hibla). The card never uses the right word, so the only definition it gives of an optical fiber reads as "thin poisons that carry visible light" — the child is left with a different thing than the English names, and nothing in the card restores it. Corpus evidence: hilo is used ~20x elsewhere in this sweep for snake/toad/jellyfish/bee venom, while the textile cards that really mean thread use tanod/hibla. Moderate-not-certain: a few other cards do use hilo for silk thread, so the corpus is not unanimous.

fact_en: Plants provide firewood, which is wood burned to make heat for cooking food and keeping homes warm.
fact_bis: Ang mga tanom nagahatag ug firewood, ang kahoy nga gisunog aron makahimo ug init sa pagluto ug pagpainit sa balay.

findings.note: title_bis "Tanom alang sa Suyop" renders "Plants for Firewood" as "Plants for Sipping/Absorbing" — suyop means to suck up, sip or absorb, never firewood (Cebuano: sugnod/gatong). Corpus evidence: 14 of the 15 cards using suyop use it for absorb/sip (tadpole tail suyopon, soil suyopon ang ulan, black absorbs light); this is the only one using it for firewood, and suyop is also in this card's terms, so the mis-mapping is systematic. The body never supplies a correct Cebuano word — it leaves "firewood" in English — so the title's Cebuano is uncorrected, and a child reading title_bis alone gets a different thing entirely.

fact_en: Objects differ from each other based on physical properties like hardness, shininess, and stretchability, which we can observe with our senses.
fact_bis: Ang mga butang magkalahi sa usag usa base sa mga physical property sama sa kagahi, pagkakasaw, ug pagka-stretchable, nga atong maobserbahan gamit ang atong mga panan-aw.

findings.note: bis: 'nga atong maobserbahan gamit ang atong mga panan-aw' — panan-aw is SIGHT, not the senses (corpus elsewhere uses igbalati/pamati/sentido, and lists panan-aw as just one of the five). The card says hardness and stretchability are observed with our eyes, and nothing in the card corrects it; a child asked how we observe physical properties answers 'sight'. Same card also garbles the second property: 'pagkakasaw' for shininess is a non-word (single occurrence in the whole sweep) where the corpus consistently says sinaw/masinaw/pagkasinaw, so 'shininess' is unrecoverable from the Cebuano.

fact_en: About half of the sun's radiation is reflected or absorbed by clouds and the atmosphere before it ever reaches the ground.
fact_bis: Mga katunga sa radiation sa adlaw ang maaninag o masuyop sa mga panganod ug atmosphere sa dili pa kini moabot sa yuta.

findings.note: EN: "About half of the sun's radiation is reflected or absorbed by clouds and the atmosphere before it ever reaches the ground." BIS: "Mga katunga sa radiation sa adlaw ang maaninag o masuyop...". In Cebuano aninag = light shining/seen THROUGH something translucent, i.e. transmission, the opposite of reflection back. This corpus uses aninag exactly that way elsewhere (ffct-15053 'Ang salamin aninag, mao nga makaagi ang kahayag'; ffct-16625 transparent; ffct-17042 translucent capiz), and renders 'reflect' as nag-reflect / mobalik / salamin everywhere else. A child reading only the Cebuano gets 'half the sun's radiation passes through or is absorbed by the clouds', so the blocked-by-reflection half is lost and nothing in the card restores it.

fact_en: Reflection means two things: the image you see in a mirror, and the property of light bouncing off a shiny surface.
fact_bis: Ang reflection adunay duha ka kahulugan: ang imahe nga makita nimo sa samin, ug ang kinaiya sa light nga mopalta gikan sa sinaw nga butang.

findings.note: Definition card for reflection: EN "the property of light bouncing off a shiny surface" -> BIS "ang kinaiya sa light nga mopalta gikan sa sinaw nga butang". Cebuano palta (< Sp. falta) = to be absent / lacking / to miss, not to bounce; the correct verbs are motalbog / mobalik (both used elsewhere in this same corpus, e.g. dcard-07322 'kung kini motalbog sa mga butang', dcard-12249 'mobalik pabalik sa gigikanan'). The card is a two-meaning definition, so the verb IS the fact: the Cebuano-only child reads 'light that goes missing from a shiny object' and cannot recover 'light bounces off'; nothing else in the card restores it. mopalta is an outlier used only 5x sweep-wide, always where bounce/reflect/slip was meant.

fact_en: Suckers are upright shoots that grow from buds at the base of a parent plant's stem, like the new shoots around a banana plant.
fact_bis: Ang suckers mao ang mga nagtindog nga shoot nga motubo gikan sa mga bud sa punoan sa parent plant, sama sa bag-ong shoot libot sa punoan sa saging.

findings.note: title_bis "Suckers sa Tungkod" for "Suckers at the Base": tungkod means a walking stick/cane, not the base of a plant. The card's own body uses the correct word ("motubo gikan sa mga bud sa punoan sa parent plant"), so the title is the outlier; a child reading the heading is told suckers grow on a cane.

fact_en:
How are bubbles made in the precipitate test?

Each mixture is halved into two small bottles, capped tightly, and shaken with the same strength and time.
fact_bis:
Unsaon paghimo ang bubbles sa precipitate test?

Ang matag mixture bahaon ngadto sa duha ka gagmay nga bottles, takpan og hugot, ug uyogon gamit ang pareho nga kusog ug oras.

findings.note: EN: "Each mixture is halved into two small bottles, capped tightly, and shaken..." BIS: "Ang matag mixture BAHAON ngadto sa duha ka gagmay nga bottles, takpan og hugot, ug uyogon..." In this very corpus 'bahaon' is the word for SNEEZE ('Ang usa ka bahaon mopakatap og liboan ka gagmayng tulo' ffct-13186; 'mobahaon' ffct-13019; 'pagbahaon' ffct-12872), while the verb for divide/split is 'bahinon' (used 44x elsewhere, e.g. 'bahinon ang tubig ngadto sa hydrogen ug oxygen'). The Cebuano procedure step therefore reads as 'each mixture is sneezed into two small bottles' -- the divide action is never named correctly anywhere on the card. Low-to-medium confidence: the trailing 'ngadto sa duha ka gagmay nga bottles' still tells the child the mixture ends up in two bottles, and the card's headline answer (bubbles come from shaking) survives, so a lenient reader could call the fact recoverable. Same defect appears on dcard-07603 ('glucose molecule nga bahaon nito'), which suggests a writer-level habit rather than a one-off typo.

fact_en: Some plants have a bad smell and taste, which are specialized structures that keep predators from eating them.
fact_bis: Ang uban nga mga tanom adunay baho ug lami, nga mga specialized structures nga makapugong sa mga predator sa pagkaon kanila.

findings.note: Title and body both render "bad smell and taste" as "baho ug lami". "Baho" carries the negative on its own, but "lami" in Cebuano means TASTY/delicious ("adunay lami" = has good flavour) — the opposite of the English "bad ... taste", and nothing in the card restores it (no pait / dili lami / walay lami anywhere). A child reads "some plants stink and taste good, and these are the structures that stop predators from eating them", which reverses the defence mechanism the card is built on. Compare dcard-04071, which correctly keeps the bad-smell sense with "baho nga baho" and never claims good taste. Fix: "baho ug pait nga lami" or "baho ug dili lami".

title_bis: Mga Timailhan sa Himsog nga Tanom
fact_en: Healthy plants have dark-green leaves and sturdy upright stems, which show that they are getting enough sunlight, water, and air.
fact_bis: Ang himsog nga mga tanom adunay itom-berde nga mga dahon ug lig-on nga tul-id nga mga sanga, nga nagpakita nga nakakuha sila ug igong kahayag sa adlaw, tubig, ug hangin.

findings.note: EN body: "Healthy plants have dark-green leaves and sturdy upright stems". The Cebuano renders "stems" as "mga sanga" — sanga is a BRANCH, a different plant part; the Cebuano stem is tangkay/punoan (and 'tangkay' is in fact sitting in this card's own terms list). Nothing else in the card restores the stem, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns the health sign is strong straight BRANCHES and would answer 'sanga' where the grade-5 ugat/tangkay/dahon lesson wants the stem.

fact_en: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive trait where blood clots very slowly or not at all, so even a small wound can be dangerous.
fact_bis: Ang hemophilia usa ka X-linked recessive trait diin ang dugo mobag-o hinay kaayo o dili gyud, busa bisan gamay nga samad mahimong delikado.

findings.note: Cebuano defines hemophilia as blood that "mobag-o hinay kaayo o dili gyud" (changes very slowly or not at all) instead of CLOTS slowly or not at all. Clotting is the whole fact of the card and is never restored elsewhere in the card, so a child gets no definition of hemophilia. Confirmed outlier: every other clotting card in the corpus uses mamuo/momuo/pagmuo (ffct-09055, same condition: "kulang sila sa gikinahanglan aron mamuo ang dugo"); dcard-05173 is the only card in the sweep using mobag-o.
